title: Roofs of the World
intro: You should spend about 20 minutes on this passage.

paras.t: A roof is more than a lid on a building. It keeps out rain, snow and sun, it holds in heat, and it often gives a building its character, so that an experienced traveller can usually tell from the shape of the roofs alone which part of the world a photograph was taken in. The shape depends mainly on three things: the climate, the materials that are available locally, and the traditions of the people who build. Over thousands of years, builders in different regions have found different solutions to the same problem, and the result is an astonishing variety of roofs, from the flat to the spired.

Flat roofs are common in dry regions, such as parts of North Africa and the Middle East, where rain is rare and heavy. A flat roof is simple and cheap to build, using beams of wood covered with layers of clay or earth, and it has an extra advantage: it is a useful space. Families dry fruit and washing there, sleep on it on hot nights, and meet their neighbours on the rooftops. In very hot places, the thick roof also keeps the rooms cool during the day. The weakness of a flat roof is that it copes badly with heavy rain, which can collect on the surface and leak through.

Where rain and snow are common, builders prefer the pitched roof, which slopes steeply from a central ridge. Water runs off it quickly and snow slides down before it becomes too heavy. In northern Europe, houses often have roofs steeper than forty-five degrees for this reason. The space under the slope, called the attic, can be used for storage or as a bedroom. Pitched roofs are covered with tiles, slates, wooden shingles or straw, according to what is available nearby; in some villages, thatch made from reeds can last for sixty years if it is carefully maintained by a skilled craftsman.

The dome, a roof shaped like half a ball, spans a wide space without columns in the middle. The Romans learned to build large domes with concrete, and the dome of the Pantheon in Rome, completed nearly nineteen centuries ago, is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world. Builders in the Islamic world and later in Renaissance Europe developed the dome further, using it for mosques, churches and public buildings. A dome has a strong shape, because the weight is spread evenly around its curve, and it also has a pleasing echo and a sense of grandeur which many architects admire. However, it is difficult and expensive to construct.

The spire is a tall, narrow roof that rises to a point. Spires appeared on churches in medieval Europe, where they pointed towards heaven and could be seen from a great distance, so that travellers could find their way to a town. Some of them are enormous: the spire of Ulm Minster in Germany is the tallest church spire in the world, at more than one hundred and sixty metres. Building such a tower required skilled stone masons and many years of work, and some projects took centuries to finish. In modern cities, glass skyscrapers sometimes borrow the same pointed form in order to catch the attention of people in the street.

In recent years, many cities have begun to plant their roofs. A green roof is covered with soil and plants, and it provides several benefits. It absorbs rainwater, reducing the danger of flooding, it keeps the building cooler in summer and warmer in winter, and it offers a home for insects and birds. Dr Lucia Moretti, an architect, says that a green roof can last twice as long as an ordinary one because the plants protect the surface from sun and frost. The main disadvantage is the weight, since wet soil is heavy, so the building must be designed to support it from the start, which raises the initial cost.

Another modern idea is the solar roof, which turns a surface that was once simply a shelter into a small power station. Panels made of silicon change sunlight into electricity, and a typical family house needs only about twenty panels to produce as much power as it uses in a year in a sunny climate. Some manufacturers now make solar tiles that look like ordinary slates, so that owners need not spoil the appearance of an old house. The cost of panels has fallen sharply in the last decade, and in many regions installing them now pays for itself within about eight years.
